scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Oyilattam originated in the Madurai region of southern Tamil Nadu, India, and developed as a rural folk expression.
Over time, it spread through southern districts including Tirunelveli and Tiruchirapalli.
The tradition was later identified for cultural mainstreaming by Tamil University to support its preservation and broader recognition.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Mainly performed during village festivals, Oyilattam also carries a practical agricultural purpose: it was danced following harvest times to deter birds from eating harvested grains laid out on the ground.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance begins with a small group of performers standing in a row, each holding two kerchiefs or with colored handkerchiefs secured to their fingers.
Dancers execute rhythmic steps that sync with the musical accompaniment.
As the dance proceeds, the row expands as additional dancers join the formation, intensifying the synchronized movements and footwork.
Watch for Kerchief waving, Expanding row progression.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical accompaniment is typically provided by the thavil drum, whose rhythmic beats direct the timing of the performance.
The percussive soundscape is augmented by the metallic chiming of ankle bells worn on the dancers' feet.
Listen for the Thavil, Ankle bells.

A dynamic percussive texture defined by the driving, acoustic strikes of the thavil drum, overlaid with the continuous metallic chiming of the dancers' ankle bells ringing out in rhythmic synchronization.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The dance is primarily performed across southern Tamil Nadu, particularly in Madurai district, Tirunelveli district, and Tiruchirapalli district.
Historically passed down as a male folk dance tradition in rural villages, the form has evolved over the past decade as women have begun performing it alongside men.
